unit: Mrs. Rachel Lynde resides with her meek husband, Thomas, in Lynde's Hollow, a location along the main road that allows her to watch all who enter or leave Avonlea. Upon spotting Matthew Cuthbert driving out in his best clothes, she visits Green Gables out of curiosity and learns that the Cuthberts plan to adopt an orphan boy. Soon after, when Marilla and Matthew decide to keep Anne Shirley instead, Mrs. Rachel visits Green Gables to inspect the child. Her blunt criticisms of Anne's freckles and red hair trigger an explosive outburst of temper from Anne, leading to a feud that resolves when Anne delivers a dramatically thorough apology. Over time, Mrs. Rachel grows fond of Anne, praising her progress and helping Matthew secure a fashionable dress with puffed sleeves for her Christmas gift. She remains a prominent community figure, active in church work, politics, and local affairs, and eventually brings word to Green Gables that Anne has been offered the Avonlea school.

I don’t believe a rose would be as nice if it was called a thistle or a skunk cabbage. I suppose my father could have been a good man even if he had been called Jedediah; but I’m sure it would have been a cross. Well, my mother was a teacher in the High School, too, but when she married father she gave up teaching, of course. A husband was enough responsibility. Mrs. Thomas said that they were a pair of babies and as poor as church mice. They went to live in a weeny-teeny little yellow house in Bolingbroke. I’ve never seen that house, but I’ve imagined it thousands of times. I think it must have had honeysuckle over the parlor window and lilacs in the front yard and lilies of the valley just inside the gate. Yes, and muslin curtains in all the windows. Muslin curtains give a house such an air. I was born in that house. Mrs. Thomas said I was the homeliest baby she ever saw, I was so scrawny and tiny and nothing but eyes, but that mother thought I was perfectly beautiful. I should think a mother would be a better judge than a poor woman who came in to scrub, wouldn’t you? I’m glad she was satisfied with me anyhow; I would feel so sad if I thought I was a disappointment to her—because she didn’t live very long after that, you see. She died of fever when I was just three months old. I do wish she’d lived long enough for me to remember calling her mother. I think it would be so sweet to say ‘mother,’ don’t you? And father died four days afterwards from fever too. That left me an orphan and folks were at their wits’ end, so Mrs. Thomas said, what to do with me. You see, nobody wanted me even then. It seems to be my fate. Father and mother had both come from places far away and it was well known they hadn’t any relatives living. Finally Mrs. Thomas said she’d take me, though she was poor and had a drunken husband. She brought me up by hand. Do you know if there is anything in being brought up by hand that ought to make people who are brought up that way better than other people? Because whenever I was naughty Mrs. Thomas would ask me how I could be such a bad girl when she had brought me up by hand—reproachful-like.

unit: Marilla Cuthbert lives at Green Gables in Avonlea with her quiet brother Matthew. Expecting to adopt an orphan boy to assist with farm duties, she is shocked when Matthew brings home an imaginative eleven-year-old girl named Anne Shirley. Though initially determined to return Anne, Marilla relents due to Matthew's quiet persistence and a reluctance to surrender the child to the harsh Mrs. Blewett. As she takes on the responsibility of raising Anne, Marilla strictly manages her education, household duties, and spiritual upbringing, frequently battling Anne's theatrical flair, daydreams, and temper. Over time, Marilla grows deeply attached to the girl, secretly taking pride in her academic successes and personal development while attempting to maintain her traditional reserve. Following the sudden death of Matthew due to a bank failure, Marilla discovers that her failing eyesight threatens her ability to keep Green Gables. unit: Matthew Cuthbert lived a quiet, unmarried life at Green Gables alongside his sister Marilla. Due to advancing age and heart trouble, he agreed to adopt a young orphan boy to assist with farm work, but drove to Bright River station to discover that an eleven-year-old girl, Anne Shirley, had been sent by mistake. Intrigued and charmed by her ceaseless chatter on the drive home, Matthew quietly insisted to Marilla that they keep her. Over the next four years, he continuously championed and spoiled Anne, giving her sweetmeats and secretly buying her a fashionable dress with puffed sleeves for Christmas. When Anne won the prestigious Avery Scholarship at Queen's Academy, Matthew expressed his deep pride in her. Shortly after her graduation, Matthew collapsed and died instantaneously at the threshold of Green Gables after reading a newspaper announcement detailing the catastrophic failure of the Abbey Bank, where all his savings were kept.

She introduced several new practices to the school, such as physical culture exercises, biweekly Friday recitations, field afternoons in the woods to study nature, and a student concert that raised money for a schoolhouse flag. She organized an advanced class after school hours to prepare students for the Queen's Academy Entrance examination. Although she considered accepting a position at a school in her home district, she chose to return to Avonlea for another year to see her Queen's class through their examinations. Under her guidance and thorough drilling, all her candidate students successfully passed the Entrance exams.
